_comment: PERFORMANCE CONTRACT. Top-level keys are the budget VALUES consumed by bench/budget_check.js, .github/workflows/check.yml and manuscript/reproduce.sh; a null value means 'no number is claimed'. Every key has a matching _meta entry saying whether it is MEASURED (and by which bench file and metric) or explicitly NOT MEASURED with the reason. tests/test_budget_coverage.js enforces that a new key with neither a producer nor a stated reason fails CI. A number here is a promise about a measurement, never a target someone hoped for.

heavy_compute_ms.measured_spread: 13.86 - 14.23 across 8 independent runs; worst single-run max 15.39
heavy_compute_ms.statistic: mean of 30 timed calls after 20 warmup; 8 independent processes
heavy_compute_ms.provenance: 2.0 in this file from 2026-09-11 to 2026-09-30 was never achievable and was never once met. `git log -p --follow bench/budget.json` shows exactly ONE commit (3ee4914, 2026-09-11), which creates the file already containing 2.0 — there is no earlier value it could have regressed from. Running that same commit's own bench/perf.js today reports 15.17 ms/compute, and its src/heavy.js run directly gives 51.2 ms at de10a73 (2026-08-11) falling to 14.1 ms now. So 2.0 was fiction at birth, not a 7x regression: the O(N) SpatialGrid work in 3ee4914 took heavy from ~51 ms to ~15 ms and the budget was written against neither number. CI has emitted '::warning Heavy compute ... exceeds budget 2.0' on every single run since, which is a permanently lit warning that gates nothing.
heavy_compute_ms.rebasis: 2026-09-30, to the measured value plus ~14% headroom. This is a REGRESSION TRIPWIRE, not a performance target: a change that pushes heavy compute past 16.0 ms trips the gate, ordinary machine-to-machine variance does not. The honest target for making heavy mode faster is tracked as an open item in ROADMAP section 4, not smuggled in here as a number the code never met.

cg_compute_ms.statistic: mean of 30 timed calls after 20 warmup; 8 independent processes
cg_compute_ms.provenance: 0.5 was reachable from birth (measured 0.174, i.e. 2.9x under budget) and is left unchanged. The heavy key next to it was 7x under the truth, which is the whole reason a sibling number nobody audited was believed for a month.

fps.reason: NOT MEASURABLE IN THIS ENVIRONMENT, and no number is claimed. A frame rate needs a frame: a canvas, a compositor, a display refresh, a GPU. This repo has zero dependencies by design (package.json has no `dependencies` block at all), there is no canvas polyfill and no jsdom, and `new Viewer({})` in bare Node throws `TypeError: canvas.getContext is not a function` because src/viewer.js binds window.addEventListener('resize') and reads devicePixelRatio at construction. requestAnimationFrame does not exist in Node either. A headless Node bench has no frame rate; asserting one would be a fabricated measurement, which is strictly worse than admitting the gap. Hence the null.
fps.what_would_measure_it: A real browser, not this repo's Node gate: tests/manual/ already holds the Playwright legs for exactly this class of check. Until such a leg exists and writes a frames/second figure to a file CI reads, no doc, script or workflow in this repo prints an fps budget.
fps.measured_neighbour: The two things a headless bench CAN say about interactivity, and does say, are in bench/perf.js: heavy compute is 14.1 ms/compute, and advance(steps, 14) caps physics at 14 ms of wall clock per animation frame (src/main.js:1454). 14.1 > 14 means heavy mode fits at most ONE force evaluation per frame at the reference position. That is a real, measured, falsifiable statement about frame pacing. It is not a frame rate and is not reported as one.
